PREFACE  
Education, no doubt, plays an important role as the foremost  effective 
channel and instrument for providing solid bases, building blocks, and 
appropriate mechanisms for economic, political, social, cultural, and overall 
national development. The current reform process in the education sector, 
anchored on the Renewed Hope Agenda  of the current administration, 
is strategic in the effort to place Nigeria on the right track for economic 
emancipation, human capital development, and social transformation.  
To attain all the lofty values of socioeconomic development and 
reconstruction enshrined in the reform initiatives , as well as those 
contained in the global agenda, including the education 2030 agenda 
encapsulated in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), there was the 
need to prioritise curriculum reform across all levels of education. Thus, 
one of the Presidential mandates for the Federal Ministry of Education , as 
exemplified in the Ministerial Deliverables , is to achieve a rapid review of 
the educational curriculum across all levels of education to ensure 
alignment with skills needed in the labour market. Furthermore, since the 
introduction of the extant Senior Secondary Education  Curriculum (SSEC) 
in 2011, t he world has witnessed tremendous transformation shaped by 
the revolution ary and evolutionary force of Information Communication 
Technology (ICT) and other social forces . There have also been emerging 
and prevailing issues in health, energy, sports, values, and all other 
aspects of human existence.  
The issues highlighted above provided a basis for the review of the 
curriculum. This is further strengthened by  an overriding vision to produce 
learners with functional, transferable, technological, vocati onal and 
entrepreneurial skills. These skills are needed for the country ’s economic 
development and individual fulfilment in a competitive globalised 
environment. Thus, the revision of the SSEC is founded on the  philosophy 
of ensuring that every senior sec ondary school graduate is well prepared 
for higher education, imbued with relevant functional skills needed for the 
work, job creation  and wealth generation ; and further empowered to 
demonstrate ethical, moral and democratic values , active citizens ’ 
participation and positive contributions for sustained growth of the nation.  
The review, which was anchored on the outcome and competency -based 
curriculum framework, commenced with a series of stakeholders ’ 
engagements, including the learners. The stakeholders ’ engagements 
culminated in the hosting of the National Stakeholders’ Dialogue and High-
Level Policy Committee (HLPC) meeting under the leadership of the 
Honourable Ministers of Education. The HLPC considered and ap proved a 
new curriculum structure with the benchmarks and standards that 
emerged from the stakeholders ’ engagements and the nationwide needs 
assessment conducted by NERDC. The new structure , which is driven b y 
the Renewed Hope Agenda of Mr  President and th e Ministerial Strategic 
Plan, the Nigerian Education Sector Renewal Initiative (NESRI) , also drew 
from the globally agreed goals. Consequently, in the new structure, apart 
from the core and compulsory subjects, there are now three fields of study 
covering Science, Humanities and Business. This new structure provides 
an opportunity for deep learning through a well -structured learning 
pathway t o prepare students for future career opportunities of  their 
choice.  
Broadly, the  goals of the new curriculum, as derived from the new 
structure, are to: 
1. Provide education that will equip the students with sound moral, 
patriotic and democratic values that will enable them to be well 
adjusted to think independently and rationally , as well as respect 
the views and feelings of others in an inclusive and progressive 
society.  
2. Provide education that will equip the students with knowledge, 
skills and the right attitude to appreciate the dignity of labour and 
the beauty of nature. 
3. Offer diversified curriculum contents to cater for differences in 
talents, dispositions and opportunities for positive contribution to 
vi 
 
society and for informed choices in vocation and/or higher 
education pursuit. 
4. Empower students for self -improvement, creativity, innovation s, 
and life-long learning to take up emerging challenges in society 
for better living. 
5. Develop in students broad-based digital and entrepreneurial skills 
and STEM/STEAM for global competitiveness, self -reliance, job 
creation and wealth generation. 
6. Equip students with 21st-century skills in all spheres of learning to 
enable them to function effectively in the world of work and in the 
global community.   
7. Promote inclusiveness and interdisciplinarity in curriculum delivery. 
Therefore, by the end of senior secondary education, all students are 
expected to:  
1. Exhibit sound moral, patriotic and democratic values in their day-
to-day life. 
2. Respect the views and feelings of others for peaceful and 
harmonious co-existence. 
3. Appreciate and preserve the beauty of nature. 
4. Adopt interdisciplinary approaches in solving societal problems and 
managing personal well-being. 
5. Make informed career choices that align with their life ambitions, 
talents, dispositions and available local and international 
opportunities. 
6. Demonstrate excellence in day-to-day activities at school and in 
society, irrespective of abilities or disabilities. 
7. Apply digital and entrepreneurial skills to create jobs and generate 
wealth. 
8. Exhibit leadership qualities and democratic ideals in societal 
conduct and group dynamics 
9. Apply 21st-century skills and STEM/ STEAM-oriented practices in 
the learning process and in daily life activities. 
10. Utilise ICT skills in all spheres of learning to function effectively in 
society and compete favourably in the global arena.  
These generic outcomes provided the basis upon which the themes and 
specific learning outcomes were developed  with specific reference to the 
subject's unique identi ties and nature . The curriculum contents are 
therefore organised around the specific learning outcomes spread across 
the thematic areas. The outcomes place clear expectations on the 
teaching and learning process, with emphasis on what the students can do 
after undergoing an instructional period. They also  inform the teachers, 
parents, examination bodies and policy makers what knowledge, skills and 
competencies the learners are expected to demonstrate at every given 
time in the instructional process. There are also competencies that the 
learners are expecte d to acquire and exhibit after being exposed to a 
series of learning experiences under a given topic. These competencies 
are not subject-specific but transversal and therefore can be acquired and 
applied across all topics in the teaching and learning proce ss. These 
competencies prepare the learners for meaningful living in all 
circumstances and across geographical divides.  
The New R evised Senior Secondary Education Curriculum is student -
centric and has integrated critical national and global issues as mean s of 
developing abilities and nurturing creative skills and other valuable skills in 
the learners. Furthermore, the curriculum provides the opportunity for  the 
teaching and learning of emerging issues like Climate change, Artificial 
Intelligence (AI), biosafety, security, robotics, peace education, and blue 
and green education. The introduction of these emerging issues and other 
core elements of learning was  based on the curriculum's fundamental 
principles of interdisciplinary learning, ethical and social responsibility, 
resilience and inclusivity. It also embodied aspects of the 21 st Century 
Skills, including critical thinking, problem solving, information l iteracy and 
vii 
 
digital skills,  communication and collaboration,  global citizenship and 
cultural awareness, creativity and innovation. Moreover, it captured issues 
of entrepreneurship, environmental and sustainability education and 
financial literacy. These issues and aspects were covered in the curriculum 
based on a systematic curriculum design process and standards that 
prevented content overload. 
The curriculum review process followed the established process of 
NERDC’s curriculum and material development, namely: 
i. Pre-design processes (including needs assessment, stakeholder 
dialogue, and setting standards) 
ii. Planning, which involves concepts/strategy formulation, 
iii. Writing/review/design, which involves the design and drafting of 
the curriculum, 
iv. Critique workshop as well as 
v. Editorial and finalisation of the curriculum documents. 
vi. Approval protocol 
A wide spectrum of stakeholders , including experts, subject matter 
specialists, teachers, teacher educators, policy makers, employers of 
labour, parents, development partners, private school owners and students 
participated at each of these stages. We acknowledge the invaluable 
contributions of these stakeholders.  
I acknowledge the efforts of the NERDC Staff who worked relentlessly to 
ensure the successful completion of the revision of the curriculum within 
the scheduled period.  I would like to posthumously acknowledge and 
appreciate my predecessor, the late Profes sor Ismail Junaidu, who 
commenced the process for developing the new curriculum prior to his 
demise in July 2024 while still in active service. 
I extend my sincere gratitude to the Honourable Minister of Education and 
Honourable Minister of State for Education for their invaluable support and 
visionary leadership in our endeavour to make education accessible to all 
Nigerian children, regardless of their circumstances.

INTRODUCTION  
The review of the Senior Secondary Education Curriculum (SSEC) was 
undertaken in response to the overdue curriculum implementation cycle, 
expansion of disciplinary knowledge, rapid technological advancement, 
evolving policy directions, and emerging global best practices. These 
contextual and developmental imperatives exert both broad and specific 
influences on the structure, focus, a nd implementation of subject 
curricula. In particular, they affect the underlying philosophy, 
methodological approach, and the selection of objectives, learning 
outcomes, content, delivery strategies, instructional resources, and 
evaluation mechanisms. 
Following the new curriculum structure, apart from the core -compulsory 
subjects, there are now three fields of study comprising Science, 
Humanities and Business.  The New Revised  Literature-in-English 
Curriculum constitutes one of the subjects in the humanities . The 
curriculum is designed to equip learners with foundational and advanced  
skills and  competencies relevant  to literary analysis and creativity . The 
curriculum is designed to achieve the following objectives: 
1. Expose students to African  and non -African literary works in 
various genres of literature 
2. Develop students’ skills in literary analysis 
3. Expand students’ vocabulary and strengthen their grammar 
through exposure to well-crafted literary texts. 
4. Enable students to connect literature with real-life situations. 
5. Encourage students’ independent judgment, interpretation, and 
appreciation of different viewpoints. 
6. Expose students to diverse cultures, traditions, and worldviews in 
literature. 
7. Teach students’ cherished values such as empathy, integrity, 
courage, and responsibility through characters and situations in 
literary works. 
8. Inspire in students original thought, creativity, and emotional 
expression. 
9. Provide students with models for creative writing and artistic 
expression. 
10. Encourage students to read for pleasure, knowledge, and personal 
enrichment. 
The curriculum adopts a competency and outcome -based approach aimed 
at developing practical and transferable skills for  productive engagement  
and lifelong learning. The competency framework cl early specifies 
performance expectations, establishes core skills benchmarks and 
promotes inclusivity in learning. It is explicitly practical  and skill-oriented, 
and results-driven. 
Furthermore, the curriculum design follows a thematic, spiral, cyclical, and 
concentric model, in which learning content is systematically sequenced, 
reinforced, and progressively deepened across class levels to align with 
students’ developmental stages an d cognitive growth. The focus of 
learning is therefore on demonstrable competencies —on what students 
can do —making the curriculum student-centred, performative, and 
achievement-oriented. This implies that the teaching and learning process 
is expected to be active, engaging and solely focused on the development 
of students ’ understanding of key concepts and the appropriate 
demonstration of necessary skills and competencies. Through this, 
students not only acquire conceptual knowledge but also and importantly , 
acquire the necessary skills for functional living in society. Thus, the 
expectations on the students go beyond classroom experiences to their 
everyday lives.

Delivery Strategy 
The effective implementation of this curriculum requires the following: 
1. Adoption of  student-centred instructional strategies that promote 
active engagement, collaboration, and creativity. 
2. Utilisation of diverse instructional resources, including digital tools 
and practical equipment, to enhance experiential and applied 
learning. 
3. Implementation of a lesson plan that integrates all essential 
elements of the new curriculum.  
4. Provision of curriculum copies to relevant teachers and school 
administrators, with emphasis on consistent and effective use. 
5. Organisation of periodic capacity -building workshops for teachers, 
supervisors, and quality assurance officers to enh ance curriculum 
interpretation and implementation competence. 
6. Alignment of assessment practices with the competency and 
outcome-based framework. 
Effective implementation of this curriculum will generate far -reaching 
benefits for Nigeria’s education system and the wider society. By equipping 
students with relevant knowledge, practical skills and core competencies, 
the curriculum will support the development of articulate, confident and 
globally competitive citizens  who would meaningfully contribut e to 
Nigeria’s socio-economic growth and development. 
Overall, this curriculum provides a transformative learning framework that 
transcends conventional classroom instruction  to empower students with 
knowledge, skills and attitudes for daily living in the 21st Century.

CATERING AND CRAFT PRACTICE SSS 2 
 
© October 2025 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
iii 
 
 
  
Nigerian Educational Research and  Development Council (NERDC)
Headquarters: Lokoja-Kaduna Road, Sheda, PMB 91, Abuja, Nigeria
Phone: (09) 8822202, 8822204, Fax (09) 8821047
iv 
 
FOREWORD 
Since Nigeria’s return to democracy over two decades ago, successive 
administrations have laid emphasis on rej uvenating the education sector 
for functionality,  socioeconomic turnaround, and over all national 
development. This is evident in the various national development plans, 
policy frameworks and management strategies that have been put in place 
to address iss ues pertaining to education. The overriding objective of 
these plans, programmes and policies, which are well -laid out, is to reform 
the education system and ensure that the target beneficiaries are well -
equipped with the requisite skills and capabilities for positive impact on 
society. However, critical stakeholders, particularly employers of labour, 
have expressed concerns about the skill set possessed by many products 
of the system. There have also been concerns raised about whether 
individuals who have undergone our educational system are adequately 
prepared for effective living in the rapidly evolving context of the 21st 
century. There is also the observed learning poverty in the system 
characterised by lack of foundational literacy and numeracy skills among a 
high percentage of learners at the basic education level. 
Consequently, at various educational and economic development fora and 
discourses, there have been consistent calls for a total reform of the 
education system for optimal performance. Addres sing these and other 
issues, and meet the demands of Nigerians, therefore, informed the 
definitive education development pathway of the Renewed Hope Agenda 
of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR.  The agenda is clear on the need 
to develop and implement a mod ern standard curriculum for the Nigeria 
education sector. The substance of the agenda is further amplified in the 
Ministerial Deliverables for the Federal Ministry of Education, which 
mandates, among others, a rapid review of the educational curriculum 
across all levels of education to align with skills needed in the labour 
market.  
Pursuant to these, we came up with several reform initiatives and well -
defined plans for the education sector including the Nigerian Education 
Sector Renewal Initiative (NESRI).  These initiatives clarify our plans and 
strategic framework for the actualization of Mr. President’s agenda for the 
education sector. They encapsulate, inter alia, development of learning 
contents that will lead to the acquisition of functional knowledge,  skills, 
and competencies. Curriculum renewal is a major action point for the 
realization and achievement of the goals and objectives of these 
initiatives. Our vision in this regard is to reform the school curriculum, 
beginning from the foundational level,  to adequately prepare our learners 
for the 21st century world.  The learner preparation, in this context, is 
broad-based covering science, technology, engineering, mathematics, 
medicine, and value reorientation. This will include building foundational 
skills in literacy and numeracy, digital skills development, citizenship and 
global awareness, entrepreneurial competence, and environmental 
literacy. 
We are delighted to state that the New Revised Basic Education 
Curriculum (BEC) has adequately covered these  issues. The curriculum is 
founded on the key pillar of preservation of our national values and 
heritage even as we strive to produce youths with global competitive 
advantages. The outcome and competency -based approach and enhanced 
delivery framework adopt ed in the design and development of this new 
curriculum is to expose our learners to a wide range, but interconnected, 
skill set and knowledge consistent with the demands of life in the 21st 
century. 
We shall therefore pursue, aggressively, its implementat ion through 
massive teacher training and orientation, provision of requisite resources 
and deployment of competent school quality assurance officers. We shall 
also invigorate and sustain the implementation process through 
collaborative efforts with the states, communities, civil society groups, and 
our development partners.  
We are aware that the development of the curriculum followed various 
stages, best practices, and broadened engagement of a range of 
stakeholders, learners, parents, education administra tors, expert and 
professional bodies, and development partners. We commend the efforts 
of the Nigerian Educational Research and Development Council (NERDC) 
v 
 
for the excellent coordination of the processes and technical inputs in the 
design of this new curri culum. We also commend all the critical 
stakeholders, members of the academia, teachers, community leaders, 
policy makers, parents and learners who participated at various stages of 
the development process.  
It is our hope that the States, relevant agencie s, and all stakeholders 
across the country will ensure effective implementation based on set out 
strategic  plan to accelerate the achievement of our desired result.  
 
 
Dr Tunji Maruf Alausa                          Professor Suwaiba Said Ahmad  
Honourable Minister of Education                   Honourable Minister of State for Education 
  
 
vi 
 
PREFACE 
Education, no doubt, plays important role as the foremost  effective 
channel and instrument for providing solid bases, building blocks, and 
appropriate mechanisms for economic, political, social, cultural, and 
overall nation’s development.  The current reform s process in the 
education sector, anchored on the Renewed Hope Agenda  of the 
current administration, is strategic in the effort to place Nigeria on the 
right track for economic emancipa tion, human capital development, and 
social transformation.  
To attain all the lofty values of socioeconomic development and 
reconstruction enshrined in the reform initiatives as well as those 
contained in global agenda, including the education 2030 agenda  
encapsulated in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), there was the 
need to prioritise curriculum reform across all levels of education. Thus, 
one of the Presidential mandates for the Federal Ministry of Education as 
exemplified in the Ministerial Del iverables, is to achieve a rapid review of 
the educational curriculum across all levels of education to ensure 
alignment with skills needed in the labour market. Furthermore, since the 
introduction of the revised 9 -Year Basic Education Curriculum (BEC) in 
2014, the world has witnessed tremendous transformation shaped by the 
revolutionary and evolutionary force of Information Communication 
Technology (ICT). There have also been emerging and prevailing issues in 
Health, Energy, Sports, Values, and all other aspects of human existence.  
The issues highlighted above provided basis for the review of the 9 -Year 
Basic Education Curriculum . This is further strengthened by  an overriding 
vision to produce learners with functional, transferable, technological, 
vocational and entrepreneurial skills. These skills are needed for the 
country’s economic development and individual fulfilment in a competitive 
globalised environment. Thus, the philosophy of the New Revised BEC is 
premised on social change, sustainable broad -based economic and 
national development through the acquisition of necessary skills, 
competencies and values.  
The review, which was anchored on the outcome and competency -based 
curriculum framework, commenced with series of stakeholders’ 
engagements includin g the learners. The stakeholders’ engagements 
culminated in hosting of the National Stakeholders’ Dialogue and High -
Level Policy Committee (HLPC) meeting under the leadership of the 
Honourable Ministers of Education. The HLPC considered and approved a 
new curriculum structure with the benchmarks and standards that 
emerged from the stakeholders’ engagements and the nationwide needs 
assessment conducted by NERDC. The new structure which is driven by 
the Renewed Hope Agenda of Mr. President and the Ministerial  Strategic 
Plan the Nigerian Education Sector Renewal Initiative (NESRI) also drew 
from the globally agreed goals.  
One outstanding feature of the new revised curriculum structure is that it 
brought about the realignment of the subject listing leading to a  reduction 
in number of subjects learners are offered across the class levels. This 
enabled the removal of redundant concepts, effective integration of 
related concepts and skills thereby eliminating the old approach to 
composite subjects. The new structure also created opportunity for the full 
introduction vocational and entrepreneurship studies at the junior 
secondary school level.  
The broad goal of the new curriculum, as derived from the new structure, 
is to inculcate in learners critical and foundation al skills and competencies 
for citizenship, social orientation, national productivity and life -long 
learning. Specifically, the curriculum is targeted at developing in learners: 
● generic social skills as well as specialised, cognitive, vocational and 
entrepreneurial skills; 
● the consciousness of our national values; 
● life-long learning; and 
● talent and skills for self-discovery and societal development. 
Within the framework of these specific targets, generic level -specific 
outcomes were formulated across the cl ass levels. At the  primary 
 
vii 
 
education level, the curriculum has been designed to help learners exhibit 
foundational knowledge, skills and competencies for: 
● reading, writing and language development; 
● the acquisition of subject matter knowledge and digital 
competencies;  
● technological, vocational and entrepreneurial trades practices;  
● problem-solving and creativity capabilities for continuing and life -
long learning; as well as 
● emotional intelligence, social values, interpersonal, leadership and 
soft skills for character development and citizenship. 
At the Junior Secondary Schools level, the curriculum is geared towards:  
● the acquisition of subject matter knowledge and competencies for 
further education at the senior secondary level; 
● technological, vocational an d entrepreneurship practices and 
training; 
● the inculcation of social values, soft skills for active and effective 
citizenship; as well as 
● talent discovery and development. 
These generic outcomes provided the basis upon which the themes and 
specific learnin g outcomes were developed. The curriculum contents are 
therefore organized around the specific learning outcomes spread across 
the thematic areas. The outcomes place clear expectations on the 
teaching and learning process with emphasis on what the learners  can do 
after undergoing an instructional period. They also inform the teachers, 
parents, examination bodies and policy makers what knowledge, skills and 
competencies the learners are expected to demonstrate at every given 
time in the instructional process . There are also competencies that the 
learners are expected to acquire and exhibit after being exposed to a 
series of learning experiences under a given topic. These competencies 
are not subject specific but transversal and therefore can be acquired and 
applied across all topics in the teaching and learning process. These 
competencies prepare the learners for meaningful living in all 
circumstances and across geographical divides.  
These generic outcomes provided the basis upon which the themes and 
specific learning outcomes were developed. The curriculum contents are 
therefore organised around the specific learning outcomes spread across 
each thematic area. The outcomes place clear expectations on the 
teaching and learning process. The stated outcomes empha sise what the 
learners can do after undergoing an instructional period. They also inform 
the teachers, parents, examination bodies and policy makers what 
knowledge, skills and competencies the learners are expected to 
demonstrate at every given time in the educational process. 
There are also competencies that the learners are expected to acquire and 
exhibit after being exposed to a series of learning experiences pertaining 
to various contents. These competencies are not subject specific but 
transversal and therefore can be acquired and applied across all topics in 
the teaching and learning process. These competencies prepare the 
learners for meaningful living in all circumstances and across geographical 
divides.

INTRODUCTION 
The Review of the Senior Secondary School (SSS) Catering and Craft 
Practice Curriculum was necessitated by emerging factors associated with 
curriculum renewal cycles, rapid technological advancements, new policy 
directions, global best practices and the dynamic nature of the hospitality 
industry. These developments have far -reaching implications for the 
structure, philosophy, and content of the subject curriculum. Specifically, 
they influence the formulation of learning objectives, outcomes, thematic 
focus, instructional approaches, resources, and assessment procedures. 
The New Revised Catering and Craft Practice Curriculum is competency 
and outcome -based, designed to equip students with practical skills, 
knowledge and entrepreneurial competencies requ ired for self -reliance, 
sustainable employment and further education in the catering and 
hospitality sector. Its competency framework establishes clear 
expectations and standards, promotes inclusivity, and fosters excellence in 
both technical and soft skil ls essential for modern hospitality practice. The 
curriculum is skill -oriented, practical, and result -driven, emphasizing 
“learning by doing” as the central pedagogical approach. 
Furthermore, the curriculum design adopts a thematic, spiral, cyclical, and 
concentric structure where concepts, skills, and competencies are 
introduced, reinforced, and expanded progressively across the class levels 
to match students ’ maturity and cognitive development. The focus is on 
the integration of knowledge, skills, and attitudes that ensure students not 
only understand catering principles but can also apply them effectively in 
real-life contexts. Thus, it is students -centered, performance -based and 
industry-relevant. 
The Catering and Craft Practice Curriculum adopts a multi disciplinary 
approach, linking knowledge from food science, home economics, 
business, and technology to develop students ’ professional and 
entrepreneurial capacities. It provides exposure to food commodities, 
culinary techniques, hospitality management, me nu planning, hygiene, 
safety, and the use of modern catering equipment and ICT tools. Students 
engage with contemporary national and global hospitality issues, 
promoting innovation, critical thinking, problem -solving, and social 
responsibility. 
The curriculum is structured around major components such as themes, 
learning outcomes, competencies, topics, performance objectives, content 
outlines, learning activities, resources, and evaluation guides. Its distinct 
features interdisciplinary, integration of ICT and emphasis on practical and 
activity-based learning enhance its relevance and global competitiveness. 
The curriculum also progressively shifts learning responsibility to the 
students, thereby nurturing autonomy, creativity, and accountability. 
Through this approach, students gain not only theoretical understanding 
but also the practical competencies needed for sustainable living and 
national development. 
Ultimately, the effective implementation of this curriculum will ensure that 
students develop the nece ssary knowledge and hands -on experience to 
function effectively as caterers, food service workers, entrepreneurs, and 
hospitality professionals. It will also promote self -reliance, career 
readiness, and global competitiveness in alignment with the goals of  
Nigeria’s Senior Secondary Education Curriculum Reform. 
General Objectives of the CCP curriculum  
The core objectives of teaching CCP in basic education are to: 
1. Develop in students Motivation and Interest in the study of 
Catering for career prospects.  
2. Equip students with knowledge of food commodities, cost, quality 
and usage. 
3. Apply cleanliness and safety precautions in food preparation, 
presentation and service delivery.    
4. Acquire emerging catering trends and global best practices   
5. Plan and execute catering and hospitality events flawlessly

Delivery/learning activities and resources 
The effective implementation of this curriculum will require that:  
1. Teachers adopt instructional strategies that will promote effective 
learner engagement and active participation. 
2. Teachers use varieties of instructional resources to promote deep and 
meaningful learning.  
3. Teachers adopt a new lesson plan that incorporates all the critical 
elements of the curriculum. A sample has been developed and 
included in the teachers’ guide.  
4. Copies of the curriculum be made available to every school teacher 
and much emphasis placed on its use in order to achieve stated 
objectives. 
5. Regular workshops are organised for teachers, supervisors and 
quality assurance officers on how to interpret and use the curriculum. 
6. Teachers adopt assessment practices that are aligned to the 
competency and outcome-based approach. NERDC has developed a 
simple to use assessment framework to support the implementation 
of curriculum. Schools and teachers should leverage on the 
framework to ensure effective assessment. 
Proper implementation of this curriculum will have far -reaching benefits 
for Nigeria's educational system and society as a whole. By equipping 
students with essential knowledge, skills and competencies prescribed in 
this curriculum, the country will produce more articulate, confident, and 
globally competitive citizens. The students will also be better prepared to 
excel in higher education and contribute meaningfully to Nigeria's 
economic and social development. 
In sum, this curriculum offers an exciting, enriching, and transformative 
journey that transcends classroom learning; it is a key to unlocking the 
limitless potential of every learner in Nigeria's classroom.

Federal Ministry of Education 
 
NEW REVISED SENIOR SECONDARY SCHOOL CURRICULUM 
FINANCIAL ACCOUNTING SSS 2 
 
© October 2025 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

iii 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Nigerian Educational Research and  Development Council (NERDC)
Headquarters: Lokoja-Kaduna Road, Sheda, PMB 91, Abuja, Nigeria
Phone: (09) 8822202, 8822204, Fax (09) 8821047
iv 
 
FOREWORD 
Our national education reform agenda under the Nigeria Education Sector 
Reform Initiative (NESRI) is driven by the overarching vision to improve 
learning outcomes and empower young people with knowledge, skills and 
competencies for national relevance and global competitiveness. A strategic 
process for achieving this is the overhaul of the school curriculum, as 
enunciated in the Renewed Hope Agenda of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, 
GCFR, which identified, as a key priority area, the development and 
implementation of a modern standard curriculum for the Nigerian education 
sector. The substance of the agenda was given impetus in the Ministerial 
Deliverables for the Federal Ministry of Education, which mandates, among 
others, a rapid review of the educational curr iculum across all levels of 
education to align with skills needed in the labour market. 
In our quest to achieve this lofty vision, we activated a strategic framework 
for the review, realignment and refocusing of all school curricula for 
functionality and relevance. The plan is to make our learners relevant and 
properly cultivated to contribut e effectively to societal development, 
leveraging the right skill set. The above underscores the need for us to move 
from the knowledge -based curriculum, which hitherto has dominated our 
educational landscape, to the competency and outcome -based curriculum 
framework with a focus on developing and deepening, in the recipients, 
critical skills for efficient performance in the world of work and productive 
engagement in the ever-changing society.  
Committed to this dream, we have been able to achieve a complete reform 
of the basic education curriculum, aligning it to the national developmental 
agenda and global standards. Logically, the next step is the review and 
remodelling of the senior secondary education curriculum to achieve proper 
linkage with the basic e ducation learning contents, as well as expand to 
learning experiences of a higher domain that match their cognitive maturity 
and societal expectations. Thus, the revised senior secondary education 
curriculum is not only competency-based but highly skill-oriented to produce 
citizens with the requisite skills for job creation and wealth generation. It 
has also fully embedded our cherished values, history and heritage to 
ensure that the learners are imbued with qualities that are fundamental for 
building a pea ceful and democratic society of choice. Furthermore, the 
curriculum has been designed to expose learners to the 21st -century skills 
for functionality in all spheres of human endeavour within and outside the 
shores of Nigeria. These features make the curric ulum unique and 
appropriate to our current needs as a nation.  
We wish to state that the development of the curriculum followed various 
stages, best practices, and broadened engagement of a range of 
stakeholders, students, parents, education administrators , experts and 
professional bodies, and development partners. We commend the efforts of 
the Nigerian Educational Research and Development Council (NERDC) for 
the excellent coordination of the processes and technical inputs in the 
design of this new curricul um. We also commend all the critical 
stakeholders, members of the academia, teachers, community leaders, 
policy makers, parents and learners who participated at various stages of 
the development process.  
We wish to reiterate our commitment to the successf ul implementation of 
the revised curriculum through extensive teacher training and orientation, 
provision of necessary resources, and deployment of competent school 
quality assurance officers. Additionally, we will sustain and invigorate the 
implementation process through collaboration with states, communities, 
civil society organisations, and development partners. 
It is our hope that the States, relevant agencies, and all stakeholders across 
the country will work together to ensure the effective implementation of the 
curriculum based on the set -out strategic plan to accelerate the 
achievement of our desired result. 
  
Dr. Tunji Maruf Alausa CON                     Professor Suwaiba Said Ahmad 
Honourable Minister of Education                  Honourable Minister of State for Education  
 
v 
 
PREFACE  
Education, no doubt, plays an important role as the foremost  effective 
channel and instrument for providing solid bases, building blocks, and 
appropriate mechanisms for economic, political, social, cultural, and overall 
national development. The current reform process in the education sector, 
anchored on the Renewed Hope Agenda of the current administration, is 
strategic in the effort to place Nigeria on the right track f or economic 
emancipation, human capital development, and social transformation.  
To attain all the lofty values of socioeconomic development and 
reconstruction enshrined in the reform initiatives, as well as those contained 
in the global agenda, including the education 2030 agenda encapsulated in 
the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), there was the need to prioritise 
curriculum reform across all levels of education. Thus, one of the 
Presidential mandates for the Federal Ministry of Education, as exemplif ied 
in the Ministerial Deliverables, is to achieve a rapid review of the educational 
curriculum across all levels of education to ensure alignment with skills 
needed in the labour market. Furthermore, since the introduction of the 
extant Senior Secondary E ducation Curriculum (SSEC) in 2011, the world 
has witnessed tremendous transformation shaped by the revolutionary and 
evolutionary force of Information Communication Technology (ICT) and 
other social forces. There have also been emerging and prevailing issues in 
health, energy, sports, values, and all other aspects of human existence.  
The issues highlighted above provided a basis for the review of the 
curriculum. This is further strengthened by  an overriding vision to produce 
learners with functional, tran sferable, technological, vocational and 
entrepreneurial skills. These skills are needed for the country ’s economic 
development and individual fulfilment in a competitive globalised 
environment. Thus, the revision of the SSEC is founded on the philosophy 
of ensuring that every senior secondary school graduate is well prepared for 
higher education, imbued with relevant functional skills needed for the work, 
job creation and wealth generation; and further empowered to demonstrate 
ethical, moral and democratic values, active citizens ’ participation and 
positive contributions for sustained growth of the nation.  
The review, which was anchored on the outcome and competency -based 
curriculum framework, commenced with a series of stakeholders ’ 
engagements, including the learners. The stakeholders ’ engagements 
culminated in the hosting of the National Stakeholders ’ Dialogue and High-
Level Policy Committee (HLPC) meeting under the leadership of the 
Honourable Ministers of Education. The HLPC considered and approved a 
new curriculum structure with the benchmarks and standards that emerged 
from the stakeholders’ engagements and the nationwide needs assessment 
conducted by NERDC. The new structure, which is driven by the Renewed 
Hope Agenda of Mr. President and the Ministerial Strategic Plan, the Nigerian 
Education Sector Renewal Initiative (NESRI), also drew from the global ly 
agreed goals. Consequently, in the new structure, apart from the core and 
compulsory subjects, there are now three fields of study covering Science, 
Humanities and Business. This new structure provides an opportunity for 
deep learning through a well -structured learning pathway to prepare 
students for future career opportunities of their choice.  
Broadly, the goals of the new curriculum, as derived from the new structure, 
are to: 
1. Provide education that will equip the students with sound moral, 
patriotic and democratic values that will enable them to be well 
adjusted to think independently and rationally, as well as respect 
the views and feelings of others in an inclusive and progressive 
society.  
2. Provide education that will equip the students with knowledge, 
skills and the right attitude to appreciate the dignity of labour and 
the beauty of nature. 
3. Offer diversified curriculum contents to cater for differences in 
talents, dispositions and opportunities for positive contribution to 
society and for informed choices in vocation and/or higher 
education pursuit. 
4. Empower students for self-improvement, creativity, innovations, 
and life-long learning to take up emerging challenges in society for 
better living. 
vi 
 
5. Develop in students broad-based digital and entrepreneurial skills 
and STEM/STEAM for global competitiveness, self-reliance, job 
creation and wealth generation. 
6. Equip students with 21st-century skills in all spheres of learning to 
enable them to function effectively in the world of work and in the 
global community.   
7. Promote inclusiveness and interdisciplinarity in curriculum delivery. 
Therefore, by the end of senior secondary education, all students are 
expected to:  
1. Exhibit sound moral, patriotic and democratic values in their day-
to-day life. 
2. Respect the views and feelings of others for peaceful and 
harmonious co-existence. 
3. Appreciate and preserve the beauty of nature. 
4. Adopt interdisciplinary approaches in solving societal problems and 
managing personal well-being. 
5. Make informed career choices that align with their life ambitions, 
talents, dispositions and available local and international 
opportunities. 
6. Demonstrate excellence in day-to-day activities at school and in 
society, irrespective of abilities or disabilities. 
7. Apply digital and entrepreneurial skills to create jobs and generate 
wealth. 
8. Exhibit leadership qualities and democratic ideals in societal 
conduct and group dynamics 
9. Apply 21st-century skills and STEM/STEAM-oriented practices in the 
learning process and in daily life activities. 
10. Utilise ICT skills in all spheres of learning to function effectively in 
society and compete favourably in the global arena.  
These generic outcomes provided the basis upon which the themes an d 
specific learning outcomes were developed with specific reference to the 
subject's unique identities and nature. The curriculum contents are 
therefore organised around the specific learning outcomes spread across 
the thematic areas. The outcomes place clear expectations on the teaching 
and learning process, with emphasis on what the students can do after 
undergoing an instructional period. They also inform the teachers, parents, 
examination bodies and policy makers what knowledge, skills and 
competencies the learners are expected to demonstrate at every given time 
in the instructional process. There are also competencies that the learners 
are expected to acquire and exhibit after being exposed to a series of 
learning experiences under a given topic. These competencies are not 
subject-specific but transversal and therefore can be acquired and applied 
across all topics in the teaching and learning process. These competencies 
prepare the learners for meaningful living in all circumstances and across 
geographical divides.  
The New Revised Senior Secondary Education Curriculum is student-centric 
and has integrated critical national and global issues as means of developing 
abilities and nurturing creative skills and other valuable skills in the learners. 
Furthermore, the curriculum provides the opportunity for the teaching and 
learning of emerging issues like Climate change, Artificial Intelligence (AI), 
biosafety, security, robotics, peace education, and blue and green education. 
The introduction of these emerging  issues and other core elements of 
learning was based on the curriculum's fundamental principles of 
interdisciplinary learning, ethical and social responsibility, resilience and 
inclusivity. It also embodied aspects of the 21 st Century Skills, including 
critical thinking, problem solving, information literacy and digital skills,  
communication and collaboration, global citizenship and cultural awareness, 
creativity and innovation. Moreover, it captured issues of entrepreneurship, 
environmental and sustainability education and financial literacy. These 
issues and aspects were covered in the curriculum based on a systematic 
curriculum design process and standards that prevented content overload. 
The curriculum review process followed the established process of NERDC’s 
curriculum and material development, namely: 
i. Pre-design processes (including needs assessment, stakeholder 
dialogue, and setting standards) 
ii. Planning, which involves concepts/strategy formulation, 
iii. Writing/review/design, which involves the design and drafting 
of the curriculum, 
iv. Critique workshop as well as 
vii 
 
v. Editorial and finalisation of the curriculum documents. 
vi. Approval protocol 
A wide spectrum of stakeholders, including experts, subject matter 
specialists, teachers, teacher educators, policy makers, employers of labour, 
parents, development partners, private school owners and students 
participated at each of these stages. We ackn owledge the invaluable 
contributions of these stakeholders.  
I acknowledge the efforts of the NERDC Staff who worked relentlessly to 
ensure the successful completion of the revision of the curriculum within the 
scheduled period. I would like to posthumously acknowledge and appreciate 
my predecessor, the late Professor Ismail Junaidu, who commenced the 
process for developing the new curriculum prior to his demise in July 2024 
while still in active service. 
I extend my sincere gratitude to the Honourable Mini ster of Education and 
Honourable Minister of State for Education for their invaluable support and 
visionary leadership in our endeavour to make education accessible to all 
Nigerian children, regardless of their circumstances. 
  
Professor Salisu Shehu  
Executive Secretary, NERDC 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
viii 
 
INTRODUCTION  
The review of the Senior Secondary Education Curriculum (SSEC) was 
undertaken in response to the overdue curriculum implementation cycle, 
expansion of disciplinary knowledge, rapid technological advancement, 
evolving policy directions, and emerging global best practices. These 
contextual and developmental imperatives exert both broad and specific 
influences on the structure, focus, and implementation of subject curricula. 
In particular, they affect the underlying philosophy, methodological 
approach, and the selection of objectives, learning outcomes, content, 
delivery strategies, instructional resources, and evaluation mechanisms. 
Following the new curriculum structure, apart from the core -compulsory 
subjects, there are now three fields of study comprising Science, Humanities 
and Business. Financial Accounting constitutes one of the subjects within 
the Business Field of Study. The curriculum is desig ned to equip learners 
with foundational and advanced skills and competencies relevant to 
Accounting and its applications. The curriculum is designed to achieve the 
following general objectives: 
1. Expose students to the concepts, principles, standards and eth ics 
of accounting. 
2. Develop in students the ability to record and classify financial 
transactions. 
3. Expose students to the preparation of financial statements. 
4. Develop in students the requisite skills needed to analyze and 
interpret financial statements. 
5. Develop in the students the requisite skills needed to use an 
accounting information system. 
The curriculum adopts a competency and outcome -based approach aimed 
at developing practical and transferable skills for productive engagement 
and lifelong learning. T he competency framework clearly specifies 
performance expectations, establishes core skills benchmarks and promotes 
inclusivity in learning. It is explicitly practical and skill-oriented, and results-
driven. 
Furthermore, the curriculum design follows a the matic, spiral, cyclical, and 
concentric model, in which learning content is systematically sequenced, 
reinforced, and progressively deepened across class levels to align with 
students’ developmental stages and cognitive growth. The focus of learning 
is the refore on demonstrable competencies —on what students can do —
making the curriculum student -centred, performative, and achievement -
oriented. This implies that the teaching and learning process is expected to 
be active, engaging and solely focused on the deve lopment of students ’ 
understanding of key concepts and the appropriate demonstration of 
necessary skills and competencies. Through this, students not only acquire 
conceptual knowledge but also and importantly, acquire the necessary skills 
for functional li ving in society. Thus, the expectations on the students go 
beyond classroom experiences to their everyday lives. 
Overview of the content coverage  
The table below provides an overview of the content coverage for the SSS 
2 Financial Accounting curriculum.

Delivery Strategy 
The effective implementation of this curriculum requires the following: 
1. Adoption of student -centred instructional strategies that promote 
active engagement, collaboration, and creativity. 
2. Utilisation of diverse instructional resources, including digital tools 
and practical equipment, to enhance experiential and applied 
learning. 
3. Implementation of a lesson plan that integrates all essential 
elements of the new curriculum.  
4. Provision of curriculum copies to relevant teachers and school 
administrators, with emphasis on consistent and effective use. 
5. Organisation of periodic capacity -building workshops for teachers, 
supervisors, and quality assurance officers to enhance curriculum 
interpretation and implementation competence. 
6. Alignment of assessment pra ctices with the competency and 
outcome-based framework. 
Effective implementation of this curriculum will generate far -reaching 
benefits for Nigeria’s education system and the wider society. By equipping 
students with relevant knowledge, practical skills and core competencies, 
the curriculum will support the development of articulate, confident and 
globally competitive citizens who would meaningfully contribute to Nigeria’s 
socio-economic growth and development. 
Overall, this curriculum provides a transfor mative learning framework that 
transcends conventional classroom instruction to empower students with 
knowledge, skills and attitudes for daily living in the 21st Century. 
 
Dr. Chima Jonas Egbujuo 
Head, Curriculum Development Centre

Phone: (09) 8822202, 8822204, Fax (09) 8821047

FOREWORD 
Since Nigeria’s return to democracy over two decades ago, successive 
administrations have laid emphasis on reju venating the education 
sector for functionality, socioeconomic turnaround, and over all national 
development. This is evident in the various national development plans, 
policy frameworks and management strategies that have been put in 
place to address issu es pertaining to education. The overriding 
objective of these plans, programmes and policies, which are well -laid 
out, is to reform the education system and ensure that the target 
beneficiaries are well-equipped with the requisite skills and capabilities 
for positive impact on society. However, critical stakeholders, 
particularly employers of labour, have expressed concerns about the 
skill set possessed by many products of the system. There have also 
been concerns raised about whether individuals who have u ndergone 
our educational system are adequately prepared for effective living in 
the rapidly evolving context of the 21st century. There is also the 
observed learning poverty in the system characterized by lack of 
foundational literacy and numeracy skills a mong a high percentage of 
learners at the basic education level. 
Consequently, at various educational and economic development fora 
and discourses, there have been consistent calls for a total reform of 
the education system for optimal performance. Address ing these and 
other issues, and meet the demands of Nigerians, therefore, informed 
the definitive education development pathway of the Renewed Hope 
Agenda of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR.  The agenda is clear 
on the need to develop and implement a mode rn standard curriculum 
for the Nigeria education sector. The substance of the agenda is further 
amplified in the Ministerial Deliverables for the Federal Ministry of 
Education, which mandates, among others, a rapid review of the 
educational curriculum across all levels of education to align with skills 
needed in the labour market.  
Pursuant to these, we came up with several reform initiatives and well-
defined plans for the education sector including the Nigerian Education 
Sector Renewal Initiative (NESRI).  These initiatives clarify our plans 
and strategic framework for the actualization of Mr. President’s agenda 
for the education sector. They encapsulate, inter alia, development of 
learning contents that will lead to the acquisition of functional 
knowledge, skills, and competencies. Curriculum renewal is a major 
action point for the realization and achievement of the goals and 
objectives of these initiatives. Our vision in this regard is to reform the 
school curriculum, beginning from the foundational level, to adequately 
prepare our learners for the 21 st century world.  The learner 
preparation, in this context, is broad -based covering science, 
technology, engineering, mathematics, medicine, and value 
reorientation. This will include building foundational skil ls in literacy 
and numeracy, digital skills development, citizenship and global 
awareness, entrepreneurial competence, and environmental literacy. 
We are delighted to state that the New Revised Basic Education 
Curriculum (BEC) has adequately covered these issues. The curriculum 
is founded on the key pillar of preservation of our national values and 
heritage even as we strive to produce youths with global competitive 
advantages. The outcome and competency -based approach and 
enhanced delivery framework adopted in the design and development 
of this new curriculum is to expose our learners to a wide range, but 
interconnected, skill set and knowledge consistent with the demands 
of life in the 21st century.  
We shall therefore pursue, aggressively, its implementat ion through 
massive teacher training and orientation, provision of requisite 
resources and deployment of competent school quality assurance 
officers. We shall also invigorate and sustain the implementation 
process through collaborative efforts with the states, communities, civil 
society groups, and our development partners.  
We are aware that the development of the curriculum followed various 
stages, best practices, and broadened engagement of a range of 
stakeholders, learners, parents, education administra tors, expert and 
professional bodies, and development partners. We commend the 
v 
 
efforts of the Nigerian Educational Research and Development Council 
(NERDC) for the excellent coordination of the processes and technical 
inputs in the design of this new curri culum. We also commend all the 
critical stakeholders, members of the academia, teachers, community 
leaders, policy makers, parents and learners who participated at 
various stages of the development process.  
It is our hope that the States, relevant agencie s, and all stakeholders 
across the country will ensure effective implementation based on set 
out strategic  plan to accelerate the achievement of our desired result. 
 
Dr Tunji Maruf Alausa               Professor Suwaiba Said Ahmad  
Honourable Minister of Education             Honourable Minister of State for Education  
 
  
vi 
 
PREFACE  
Education, no doubt, plays important role as the foremost  effective 
channel and instrument for providing solid bases, building blocks, and 
appropriate mechanis ms for economic, political, social, cultural, and 
overall nation ’s development.  The current reform s process in the 
education sector, anchored on the Renewed Hope Agenda  of the 
current administration, is strategic in the effort to place Nigeria on the 
right track for economic emancipation, human capital development, 
and social transformation.  
To attain all the lofty values of socioeconomic development and 
reconstruction enshrined in the reform initiatives as well as those 
contained in global agenda, includi ng the education 2030 agenda 
encapsulated in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), there was 
the need to prioritise curriculum reform across all the levels of 
education. Thus, one of the Presidential mandates for the Federal 
Ministry of Education as exemplified in the Ministerial Deliverables is to 
achieve a rapid review of the educational curriculum across all levels of 
education to ensure alignment with skills needed in the labour market. 
Furthermore, since the introduction of the revised Basic Educat ion 
Curriculum (BEC) in 2014, the world has witnessed tremendous 
transformation shaped by the revolution ary and evolutionary force of 
Information Communication Technology (ICT). There have also been 
emerging and prevailing issues in health, energy, sports,  values, and 
all other aspects of human existence.  
The issues highlighted above provided basis for the review of the 9 -
Year Basic Education Curriculum . This is further strengthened by  an 
overriding vision to produce learners with functional, transferable,  
technological, vocational and entrepreneurial skills. These skills are 
needed for the country ’s economic development and individual 
fulfilment in a competitive globalized environment. Thus, the 
philosophy of the new 9 -Year BEC is premised on social change , 
sustainable broad-based economic and national development through 
the acquisition of necessary skills, competencies and values.  
The review, which was anchored on the outcome and competency -
based curriculum framework, commenced with series of stakeholder s’ 
engagements including the learners. The stakeholders ’ engagements 
culminated in hosting of the National Stakeholders’ Dialogue and High-
Level Policy Committee (HLPC) meeting under the leadership of the 
Honourable Ministers of Education. The HLPC considered and approved 
a new curriculum structure with the benchmarks and standards that 
emerged from the stakeholders ’ engagements and the nationwide 
needs assessment conducted by NERDC. The new structure which is 
driven by the Renewed Hope Agenda of Mr. Presid ent and the 
Ministerial Strategic Plan the Nigerian Education Sector Renewal 
Initiative (NESRI) also drew from the globally agreed goals.  
One outstanding feature of the new curriculum structure is that it 
brought about the realignment of the subject listi ng leading to a 
reduction in number of subjects learners are offered across the class 
levels. This enabled the removal of redundant concepts, effective 
integration of related concepts and skills thereby eliminating the old 
approach to composite subjects. T he new structure also created 
opportunity for the full introduction vocational and entrepreneurship 
studies at the junior secondary school level.  
The broad goal of the new curriculum, as derived from the new 
structure, is to inculcate in learners’ critical and foundational skills and 
competencies for citizenship, social orientation, national productivity 
and life -long learning. Specifically, the curriculum is targeted at 
developing in learners: 
● generic social skills as well as specialised cognitive, vocati onal 
and entrepreneurial skills; 
● the consciousness of our national values; 
● life-long learning; and 
● talent and skills for self-discovery and societal development. 
Within the framework of these specific targets, generic level -specific 
outcomes were formulate d across the class levels. At the  primary 
vii 
 
education level, the curriculum has been designed to help learners 
exhibit foundational knowledge, skills and competencies for: 
1. reading, writing and language development; 
2. the acquisition of subject matter knowledge  and digital 
competencies;  
3. technological, vocational and entrepreneurial trades practices;  
4. problem-solving and creativity capabilities for continuing and 
life-long learning; as well as 
5. emotional intelligence, social values, interpersonal, leadership 
and soft skills for character development and citizenship. 
At the Junior Secondary Schools level, the curriculum is geared 
towards:  
6. the acquisition of subject matter knowledge and competencies 
for further education at the senior secondary level; 
7. technological, vocational and entrepreneurship practices and 
training; 
8. the inculcation of social values, soft skills for active and 
effective citizenship; as well as 
9. talent discovery and development. 
These generic outcomes provided the basis upon which the themes 
and s pecific learning outcomes were developed. The curriculum 
contents are therefore organized around the specific learning outcomes 
spread across the thematic areas. The outcomes place clear 
expectations on the teaching and learning process with emphasis on 
what the learners can do after undergoing an instructional period. They 
also inform the teachers, parents, examination bodies and policy 
makers what knowledge, skills and competencies the learners are 
expected to demonstrate at every given time in the instru ctional 
process. There are also competencies that the learners are expected 
to acquire and exhibit after being exposed to a series of learning 
experiences under a given topic. These competencies are not subject 
specific but transversal and therefore can be  acquired and applied 
across all topics in the teaching and learning process. These 
competencies prepare the learners for meaningful living in all 
circumstances and across geographical divides.

The New Revised Basic Educati on Curriculum (BEC) is learner -centric 
and has integrated critical national and global issues as means of 
developing abilities and nurturing creative skills and other valuable

emerging issue s like; Climate change, Artificial Intelligence (AI),

INTRODUCTION  
The review of the Senior Secondary Education Curriculum (SSEC) was 
undertaken in response to the overdue curriculum implementation cycle, 
expansion of disciplinary knowledge, rapid technological advancement, 
evolving policy directions, and emerging global best practices. These 
contextual and developmental imperatives exert both broad and specific 
influences on the structure, focus, and implementation of subject curricula. 
In particular, they affect the underlying philosophy, methodological 
approach, and the selection of objectives, learning outcomes, content, 
delivery strategies, instructional resources, and evaluation mechanisms. 
Following the new curriculum structure, apart from the core -compulsory 
subjects, there are now three fields of study comprising Science, Humanities 
and Business. Commerce constitutes one of the subjects within the Business 
Field of Study. The curriculum is de signed to equip learners with 
foundational and advanced skills and competencies relevant to commercial 
activities. The curriculum is designed to achieve the following general 
objectives: 
1. Equip students with fundamental understanding of the nature, 
scope and functions of commerce for potential careers in 
commerce or related fields. 
2. Enhance digital and financial literacy among students for effective 
participation in digital economy and financial inclusion.    
3. Inculcate in students knowledge and skills for effective utilization of 
services that facilitate commercial activities  
4. Instil in students the skills necessary to understand and uphold 
ethical standards and social responsibilities in commercial activities. 
5. Foster in students entrepreneurial awareness and skills for 
creativity, innovation and self-reliance. 
The curriculum adopts a competency and outcome -based approach aimed 
at developing practical and transferable skills for  productive engagement  
and lifelong learning. The compe tency framework clearly specifies 
performance expectations, establishes core skills benchmarks and promotes 
inclusivity in learning. It is explicitly practical and skill-oriented, and results-
driven. 
Furthermore, the curriculum design follows a thematic, s piral, cyclical, and 
concentric model, in which learning content is systematically sequenced, 
reinforced, and progressively deepened across class levels to align with 
students’ developmental stages and cognitive growth. The focus of learning 
is therefore o n demonstrable competencies —on what students can do —
making the curriculum student-centred, performative, and achievement -
oriented. This implies that the teaching and learning process is expected to 
be active, engaging and solely focused on the development of students ’ 
understanding of key concepts and the appropriate demonstration of 
necessary skills and competencies. Through this, students not only acquire 
conceptual knowledge but also and importantly, acquire the necessary skills 
for functional living in society. Thus, the expectations on the students go 
beyond classroom experiences to their everyday lives.

Delivery Strategy 
The effective implementation of this curriculum requires the following: 
1. Adoption of student-centred instructional strategies that promote 
active engagement, collaboration, and creativity. 
2. Utilisation of diverse instructional resources, including digital tools 
and practical equipment, to enhance experiential and applied 
learning. 
3. Implementation of a lesson plan that integrates all essential 
elements of the new curriculum.  
4. Provision of curri culum copies to relevant teachers and school 
administrators, with emphasis on consistent and effective use. 
5. Organisation of periodic capacity -building workshops for teachers, 
supervisors, and quality assurance officers to enhance curriculum 
interpretation and implementation competence. 
6. Alignment of assessment practices with the competency and 
outcome-based framework. 
Effective implementation of this curriculum will generate far -reaching 
benefits for Nigeria’s education system and the wider society. By equipping 
students with relevant knowledge, practical skills and core competencies, 
the curriculum will support the development of articulate, confident and 
11 
 
globally competitive citizens who would meaningfully contribute to Nigeria’s 
socio-economic growth and development. 
Overall, this curriculum provides a transformative learning framework that 
transcends conventional classroom instruction  to empower students  with 
knowledge, skills and attitudes for daily living in the 21st Century.
